gap: No result ChatGPT got states that on maker stores on 2026-11-14 the cheapest model meeting ChatGPT's own 3,000-lumen bar, the Epson EpiqVision Flex CO-W01 at $399.99 on epson.com, costs $79 less than the battery-powered XGIMI MoGo 4 ($479 on us.xgimi.com, 450 ISO lumens) while rated for 6.7× the light. The Epson works out to about $0.13 per lumen and the XGIMI to $1.06.
standout_why: Of the cited rivals, picks.beecommercer.com (updated 2026-11-08) lists ratings for 10 models (Capsule 3 Laser 300 ANSI, CO-FH02 3,000 ISO, GV50 500 ANSI and others) but no prices at all. rottenwifi.com (cited) would not load: one timeout and one HTTP 502. However, projectorverdict.com (uncited, rank 3) already pairs prices with lumens: Epson EX3280 at ~$399.99 for 3,600 lumens against Nebula Capsule 3 Laser at ~$799 for ~300. So the point that a $400 Epson out-lights a battery mini costing more is already partly on a page ChatGPT got. That page does not cover the CO-W01, CO-FH02, MoGo 4 or Aurzen ZIP Pro, and none of the pages has maker-store prices dated today. ChatGPT's $983.83 card for the PowerLite 1781W is $83.84 above Epson's own $899.99 (techradar returned only its title, so it could not be checked).
decides: This confirms ChatGPT's lean toward the Epson Flex models over battery minis for lit meeting rooms. On today's maker prices the 3,000-lumen Epsons ($399.99 and $499.99) are not dearer than the 450–550-lumen battery projectors ($479–$669), so lower price no longer argues for the minis. The minis win only when there is no outlet. It also undercuts the 1781W card: Epson sells it for $899.99, not $983.83, and at that price it is still WXGA with one HDMI port.
